sections.title: iCanWork: Steps to Support Cancer Survivors with Return to Work

content.text: iCanWork is a framework (1, 2) adapted for primary care providers by primary care providers, psychosocial and rehabilitation specialists, medical oncology specialists, and cancer survivors to support planning for and fostering a successful return to work (RTW).

The iCanWork program is flexible and can be tailored to meet the unique needs of any given cancer survivor. Steps may be done simultaneously or in a different order based on the primary care provider’s assessment and needs of the cancer survivor.
iCanWork steps include:
Assessment
1.   Understand factors that can impact work
2.   Assess function*
3.   Understand job demands*
Addressing Challenges
4.   Identify, treat, and refer to support*
5.   Encourage survivors to take control
Transitioning to the Workplace
6.   Identify and foster workplace supports
7.   Contribute to the development of a return to work plan
8.   Prepare survivors for imminent return to work
9.   Manage work expectations
10. Monitor the work situation
Communication is the central tenant of the iCanWork framework.
Effective communication is central to iCanWork and is integrated into each step of the iCanWork framework to support cancer survivors’ return to work (RTW).
Click on the tabs below to learn more about considerations for communicating with each of the following:
Cancer Survivor
Other Healthcare Providers
Insurance Provider
Employer/Workplace

Ideally, communication with cancer survivors about work starts at the time of diagnosis and continues at least one year after RTW. Discussing cancer survivors’ work-related abilities and concerns provides an opportunity for primary care providers to explore and facilitate improving work ability, and to determine and foster workplace support.
At Diagnosis
To aid RTW planning, cancer survivors need to initially know:(1)
The potential impact of cancer and its treatment on functional outcomes and work ability (current and over time)
Current expected work ability (duration, part-time vs. full-time, function)
Possible opportunities for improving work ability (symptom management)
Expected recovery and RTW timelines including potential delays
Restrictions or limitations that require accommodations, alternative work, or disability/sick leave if available to them
During Treatment and After Treatment

Ongoing assessment and communication are needed to determine the severity of cancer- and treatment-related sequelae during and after treatment to identify if the individual can remain working, has achieved maximum recovery, or if temporary or permanent accommodations are needed. Consider advanced planning for RTW among those identified as needing work modifications, alternative work at the same work site, or needing to find other work at another worksite and/or in a different field.
Addressing Survivor Concerns
Cancer survivors may be reluctant to RTW for a myriad of reasons. It is, therefore, important to explore current and anticipated barriers to RTW and develop a plan to address them.
Click on the cards below to reveal ways to address common concerns of survivors:
CONCERN
“I worry that I won’t be productive enough, let my colleagues down, and pretty much fail at work”
CONCERN
“I get anxious just thinking about the stress I used to feel in the workplace. I don’t think going back to work is the healthy choice for me.”
CONCERN
“I don’t know if I’m ready.”
CONCERN
“Work just doesn’t seem as important as it used to…”
CONCERN
“My boss never liked me; there’s no way I’m going to get the support I need.”
PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ACTION
Advise that a graduated return to work trial is a way to condition and rehabilitate on the job, and they do not need to have fully recovered when they start back at work.
Assure the survivor that the plan can be revised as needed.
PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ACTION

Consider referral to counselling to further explore and address psychosocial factors that are perceived as barriers to work (i.e., relationship issues, psychological factors, change in priorities, etc.)
PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ACTION
Refer or make recommendations for assessment to determine work readiness.
Advise the survivor that you will closely monitor them during and after they return to work as part of a plan to address their concerns.
PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ACTION
Suggest the cancer survivor  consult with a vocational rehabilitation counsellor or an oncology counsellor.
Discuss how prolonged work absence for cancer survivors can mean lost attachments to the workplace, losing skills and increasing the difficulty with returning to work.
PRIMARY CARE PROVIDER ACTION
Encourage the survivor to ask for support from human resources, disability management, or union representative.
Refer or make recommendations to insurance providers to

obtain support at the workplace, such as occupational therapy and vocational rehabilitation,  to assess and address challenges at the workplace (e.g., need for workplace accommodations, negotiating a supportive workplace, interpersonal issues).
Cancer Survivor
Other Healthcare Providers
Insurance Provider
Employer/Workplace

Primary care providers, oncology team members, medical specialists,  and allied health professionals can help cancer survivors create realistic expectations of a survivor’s function, and better understand and appreciate the changes needed to accept and manage these changes. (1) This may include discussing current and expected function and work ability over time (including  whether returning to the former work role is feasible), expected recovery and timelines, ways to improve work ability, and restrictions and limitations to be accommodated.

Planning collaboratively with other allied healthcare providers and work specialists will more likely result in a successful RTW and ensure the survivor receives consistent messaging about return to work.
Cancer Survivor
Other Healthcare Providers
Insurance Provider
Employer/Workplace

In many cases, long term disability insurance providers ask primary care providers to provide opinions on whether a cancer survivor can engage in work. Medical opinions around working must be determined to the best of the clinician’s knowledge and be based on the individual’s current clinical and functional information.
The primary care provider’s opinion may be used by the insurance provider to:
Determine Appropriateness of Return to Work
Evaluate whether the cancer survivor can work vs. the need to remain on disability insurance (short- or long-term).
Assess whether the survivor is able to work at their own occupation or “own occ” to determine eligibility for long-term disability insurance, often for the first two years.

Assess whether the survivor is able to work at any occupation or “any occ” to determine eligibility for long-term disability insurance (often beyond two years)  and Canada Pension Plan Disability or Québec Pension Plan Disability.
Assess Return to Work Ability & Needs
Provide timelines for reassessment or RTW trial and specify if RTW with or without required accommodations.
Consider ability to complete required volume of work over a period of time, predictability, accuracy, and harmoniously. (2)
If needed, recommend that insurance provider provides work capacity assessments, worksite support services, and guidance on compensatory strategies and job accommodations.
Facilitate Referrals to Support Recommendations
Support statements referring to  or including  specialist consultations, specific assessments, survivor self-report forms.
Qualify chart notes to indicate that medical status does not equate to functional status or work ability.
Address Treatment Compliance

Advise cancer survivors that insurance providers expect full participation in medically-recommended treatments, counselling, rehabilitation, and vocational rehabilitation to qualify for continued benefits.
State any reasonable refusal to participate in medically-recommended treatments and services in an individual's chart and on insurance forms to prevent loss of benefits.
Completing Insurance Forms

Insurance forms do not always inquire about the full scope of restrictions and limitations that affect work ability. It is of the utmost importance to include all relevant information on forms to ensure that the insurance provider is obtaining a holistic view of the cancer survivor’s challenges.
Best practices for providers to consider when filling out insurance forms:
Explain why you are qualified to write this letter and how long you have known the survivor.
Provide a detailed overview of the treatment plan.
Support your opinion with specialist consultations, specific assessments, and survivor self-reports forms.
Recommend insurance-funded assessment or interventions to support RTW, if needed.
Indicate the nature of the disability and how this impacts work function.
Discuss work restrictions and limitations.
Describe RTW as a trial to ensure that parties recognize that successful RTW cannot fully be predicted and needs to be designed with flexibility.
Provide updated notes indicating revisions if the survivor is not able to RTW on the estimated return date.
Provide recommendations for accommodations.
Indicate a schedule for monitoring progress.

Be mindful that insurance providers may not seek a primary care provider’s opinion on survivor work ability. Instead, provider medical notes can be used to determine eligibility for benefits. It is therefore important to qualify chart notes by indicating that medical status does not equate to functional status or work ability.
Cancer Survivor
Other Healthcare Providers
Insurance Provider
Employer/Workplace

Ongoing communication with employers through all stages of recovery is critical to RTW. As the return grows closer, it is crucial that all parties have an understanding of the cancer survivor’s physical, psychological, cognitive, and functional abilities and limitations. This understanding will help the employer and employee collaborate in shared planning to set realistic goals and prepare the workplace.
Steps to Communicating with a Survivor’s Employer
Employers may request that primary care providers complete a form or provide a letter indicating that the survivor is cleared to RTW and provide a plan. This form or letter needs to include:
An itemized list of restrictions and limitations relevant to the job with prompts to consider accommodations as needed
Recommendations for reasonable work-site accommodations

It is ideal to review all recommendations with the cancer survivor prior to submitting forms to the employer. You will also need to obtain written consent from the survivor before providing the employer with any information. Once a form has been sent to the employer, the primary care provider can provide ongoing recommendations as needed.
What the Employer Has a Right to Know
Diagnosis, prognosis, and how it manifests as a disability
Permanent or temporary nature of disability/illness
Restrictions or limitations caused by the disability that are associated with duties
Treatment or intervention plan as it relates to work duties and demands
Approximated timeline or dates for the return to work trial

pages.title: An Introduction to Cancer Survivorship and Return to Work
pages.content:
Many cancer survivors express a strong desire to return to work (RTW) following a diagnosis and treatment for cancer. RTW can be viewed as a symbol of recovery.1 In addition to being a positive distraction from cancer and a way to regain a normal life,2 RTW provides a sense of meaning and accomplishment, enhances self-worth and quality of life, is a means of social connection, and reduces financial hardships.

References

  1. Spelten ER, Sprangers MA, Verbeek JH. Factors reported to influence the return to work of cancer survivors: a literature review. Psychooncology. 2002;11(2):124-131.
  2. Kennedy F, Haslam C, Munir F, Pryce J. Returning to work following cancer: a qualitative exploratory study into the experience of returning to work following cancer. Eur J Cancer Care (Engl). 2007;16(1):17-25.

pages.title: Return to Work by the Numbers
pages.content:
Text description: Infographic ▼

Return to Work: By the Numbers
  • While studies show that 63.5% of cancer survivors return to work, one in five cancer survivors will likely experience cancer-related health impairments affecting their work ability.1
Impacts to Return to Work
  • 26% to 53% of cancer survivors will experience job loss or will resign during or after treatment.2-4
  • Over 26% of cancer survivors reported deterioration in their physical work ability and 19% in their mental work ability.5
  • Of the cancer survivors who return to work, 57% reduced their work hours by more than 4 hours/week (mean reduction of 15.6 hours/week), and this reduction was attributed to cancer.6

References

  1. Taskila T, Lindbohm ML. Factors affecting cancer survivors’ employment and work ability. Acta Oncol. 2007;46(4):446-451.
  2. van Egmond MP, Duijts SF, Scholten AP, van der Beek AJ, Anema JR. Offering a tailored return to work program to cancer survivors with job loss: a process evaluation. BMC Public Health. 2016;16(1):1-16.
  3. Choi KS, Kim E-J, Lim J-H, et al. Job loss and reemployment after a cancer diagnosis in Koreans - a prospective cohort study. Psychooncology. 2007;16(3):205-213.
  4. Mehnert A. Employment and work-related issues in cancer survivors. Crit Rev Oncol Hematol. 2011;77(2):109-130.
  5. Taskila T, Martikainen R, Hietanen P, Lindbohm M-L. Comparative study of work ability between cancer survivors and their referents. Eur J Cancer. 2007;43(5):914-920.
  6. Steiner JF, Cavender TA, Nowels CT, et al. The impact of physical and psychosocial factors on work characteristics after cancer. Psychooncology. 2008;17(2):138-147.

Effective communication is central to iCanWork and is integrated into each step of the iCanWork framework to support cancer survivors' return to work (RTW).

The Role of Primary Care

To best support cancer survivors' RTW, primary care providers are encouraged to facilitate and engage in conversations with cancer survivors, insurance providers, the survivor's employer/workplace, health care professionals, and others.

Click on the tabs below to learn more about considerations for communicating with each of the following:

        •  Cancer Survivor
        •  Other Healthcare Providers
        •  Insurance Provider
        •  Employer/Workplace

Discussing cancer survivors’ work-related abilities and concerns provides an opportunity for primary care providers to explore and facilitate improving work ability, and to determine and foster workplace support.

At diagnosis

To aid RTW planning, cancer survivors need to initially know:1

  • The potential impact of cancer and its treatment on functional outcomes and work abilities (current and over time)
  • Current expected work ability (duration, part-time vs. full-time, function)
  • Possible opportunities for improving work ability (symptom management)
  • Expected recovery and RTW timelines including potential delays
  • Restrictions or limitations that require accommodations, alternative work, or disability/sick leave if available to them

Concern

I worry that I won’t be productive enough, let my colleagues down, and pretty much fail at work

Assure survivor that the plan can be revised as needed.

I don’t think going back to work is the healthy choice for me

Primary Care Provider Action

Concern

Primary Care Provider Action

Refer or make recommendations for assessment to determine work readiness.

Advise the survivor that you will closely monitor them during and after they RTW as part of a plan to address their concerns.

Concern

Cancer and Work: Roles of Professionals

In many cases, long term disability insurance providers ask primary care providers to provide opinions on whether an individual can engage in work. Medical opinions around working must be determined to the best of the clinician’s knowledge and be based on the cancer survivor's current clinical and functional information.

A primary care provider's opinion may be used by the insurance provider to:

    1. Determine Appropriateness of Return to Work ▼

  • Evaluate whether the cancer survivor can work vs. the need to remain on disability insurance (short- or long-term).
  • Assess whether the survivor is able to work at their own occupation or “own occ” to determine eligibility for long-term disability insurance (often beyond two years), often for the first two years.
  • Assess whether the survivor is able to work at any occupation or “any occ” to determine eligibility for long-term disability insurance and Canada Pension Plan Disability or Québec Pension Plan Disability.

Clinical Tip

Long-term disability providers are often open to funding private care supports that can expedite the RTW process, if recommended by a primary care provider. Supports may include counselling, occupational therapy support, neuropsychology, and cancer exercise programs.

    1. Assess Return to Work Ability & Needs ▼

  • Provide timelines for reassessment or RTW trial and specify if RTW with or without required accommodations.
  • Consider ability to complete required volume of work over a period of time, predictability, accuracy, and harmoniously.2
  • If needed, recommend that insurance provider provides work capacity assessments, worksite support services, and guidance on compensatory strategies and job accommodations.

Clinical Tip

To help assess readiness and support for RTW, primary care providers can recommend that the insurance provider fund work capacity evaluation, work-site supports, and other treatment supports. In addition to this, insurance providers should be encouraged to fund rehabilitation professionals who can provide guidance on compensatory strategies, recommend job accommodations, and help negotiate RTW with employers.

    1. Facilitate Referrals to Support Recommendations ▼

  • Support statements referring to or including specialist consultations, specific assessmentsExamples: oncology reports, psychological assessments, and rehabilitation assessments, and survivor self-report forms.
  • Qualify chart notes to indicate that medical status does not equate to functional status or work ability.

Clinical Tip

In certain cases (e.g. prolonged psychological challenges), insurance providers may defer to in-house medical expert opinions. In these situations, if primary care providers have concerns, they can opt to refer to a specialist or make recommendations for insurance providers to seek out experts who can support in the accurate assessment of work ability and readiness.

    1. Address Treatment Compliance ▼

  • Advise cancer survivors that insurance providers expect full participation in medically-recommended treatments, counselling, rehabilitation, and vocational rehabilitation to qualify for continued benefits.
  • State any reasonable refusal to participate in medically-recommended treatments and services in an individual's chart and on insurance forms to prevent loss of benefits.
Completing Insurance Forms

Insurance forms do not always inquire about the full scope of restrictions and limitations that affect work ability. It is of the utmost importance to include all relevant information on forms to ensure that the insurance provider is obtaining a holistic view of the cancer survivor’s challenges.

Clinical Tip

If the insurance form does not leave enough room or does not ask the right question, you may add additional notes on the front or back of the form.

Best practices for providers to consider when filling out insurance forms include:

    • Explain why you are qualified to write this letter and how long you have known the cancer survivor.
    • Provide a detailed overview of the treatment plan.
    • Support your opinion with specialist consultations, specific assessments, and survivor self-report forms.
    • Recommend insurance-funded assessment or interventions to support RTW, if needed.
    • Indicate the nature of the disability and how this impacts work function.
    • Discuss work restrictions and limitations.
    • Describe RTW as a trial ensuring that parties recognize that successful RTW cannot fully be predicted and needs to be designed with flexibility.
    • Provide updated notes indicating revisions if the survivor is not able to RTW on the estimated return date.
    • Provide recommendations for accommodations.
    • Indicate a schedule for monitoring progress.
    • Be mindful that insurance providers may not seek a primary care provider’s opinion on survivor work ability. Instead, provider medical notes can be used to determine eligibility for benefits. It is therefore important to qualify chart notes by indicating that medical status does not equate to functinal status or work ability.

by Faith Hayman, trial, appellate, and long-term disability lawyer (34 mins)

Ongoing communication with employers through all stages of recovery is critical to RTW. As the return grows closer, it is crucial that all parties have an understanding of the cancer survivor’s physical, psychological, cognitive, and functional abilities and limitations. This understanding will help the employer and employee collaborate in shared planning to set realistic goals and prepare the workplace.

The Role of Primary Care

The primary care provider’s role in supporting a cancer survivor’s early and safe RTW is to provide continuing, accurate, and detailed medical information and its impact on function at work. With this information, the employer is better equipped to address medically required restrictionsRestrictions are defined by what the cancer survivor should not do on the basis of risk of harm to self or others. and limitationsLimitations are defined by what the cancer survivor lacks in current abilities and/or skills., and provide appropriate accommodations.

Steps to Communicating with Survivor’s Employer

Employers may request that primary care providers complete a form or provide a letter indicating that the survivor is cleared to RTW. This form or letter needs to include:

  • An itemized list of restrictions and limitations relevant to the job with prompts to consider accommodations as needed
  • Recommendations for reasonable work-site accommodations An employer has a duty to reasonably accommodate on an ongoing basis those with a disability unless the employer can prove undue hardship. The duty to accommodate means that employers must implement the necessary measures that will allow employees with limitations due to illness or disability to work to the best of their ability. The principle of accommodations to the needs of people with an illness or disability includes cancer survivors.

    Be aware that the employer ultimately has the duty to determine accommodation based on restrictions and limitations outlined from the medical information. If accommodations cannot be met by the employer, there may be a risk of job loss. For more information see Cancer and Work: Reasonable Accommodation

It is ideal to review all recommendations with the cancer survivor prior to submitting forms to the employer. You will also need to obtain written consent from the survivor before providing the employer with any information. Once a form has been sent to the employer, the primary care provider can provide ongoing recommendations as needed.

Employers may request a Fitness for Return to Work or Fit for Work form. On this form, primary care providers will need to indicate that the survivor is ready to return on a specified date. Additionally, it is helpful to itemize the restrictions and limitations ensuring employers are aware of accommodations that need to be planned.

What the Employer Has a Right to Know
  • Diagnosis, prognosis, and how it manifests as a disability
  • Permanent or temporary nature of disability/illness
  • Restrictions or limitations caused by the disability that are associated with duties
  • Treatment or intervention plan as it relates to work duties and demands
  • Approximated timeline or dates for the RTW trial

pages.title: The Role of Primary Care
pages.content:
Primary care providers play a significant role in addressing issues cancer survivors may experience and in helping foster successful return to work (RTW).

The Canadian Medical Association (CMA) guidelines for supporting general RTW indicate that primary care providers play an important role by:

Diagnosing and treating illness or injury

Advising and supporting the patient

Providing and communicating appropriate information
to the patient and employer

 

Working closely with other involved healthcare professionals
to facilitate the patient’s safe and timely return to the most productive employment possible

This course will explore the practical application of the roles outlines by the CMA within the context of supporting cancer survivors' RTW.

Resources

CMA Policy: The Treating Physician’s Role in Helping Patients Return to Work After an Illness or Injury

sections.title: iCanWork Step 1: Understand factors that can impact work

content.text: There are many factors that impact a cancer survivor's chances for a successful return to work (RTW). Understanding the facilitators that can ease, and the barriers that can hinder RTW can help determine areas that need to be addressed to facilitate the survivor’s successful RTW.
The Vocational Rehabilitation Model for Cancer Survivors (1) identifies four factors that providers should consider and explore when supporting a cancer survivor’s RTW:
Click on each of the four factors to learn more:
Bio-psychological                                  Person-related                                          System                                                    Worksite
Bio-psychological factors include all the biological and psychological factors that can proceed, emerge, or continue after diagnosis and treatment. Examples include:
Pre-existing conditions and disabilities
Cancer disease and treatment-specific factors
Short-term, late, and long-term effects of cancer and treatment
Scenarios:
A cancer survivor now finds that the neuropathy in his hands is not improving, and finds himself no longer able to type on a keyboard.

Due to pre-existing learning difficulties unrelated to cancer, a cancer survivor has previously chosen to work as a labourer. She is now unable to do the heavy work required for this job but does not think she can undertake formal schooling because of her learning challenges.

A cancer survivor who has previously worked as a manager now experiences ongoing problems with low mood, concentration, word-finding, and memory, and feels managing others in a busy work setting is now challenging.

Many cancer survivors describe a change in meaning, priorities, and motivation with work. Person-related factors are unique to the individual and can impact the ability, willingness, and access to RTW. Examples include:
Demographics (age, gender, race, education)
Perception of work environment and culture
Expectations of health recovery, return to work, and work ability
Socioeconomic status
Scenarios:

A cancer survivor feels that stress caused their cancer and feels that the main source of stress comes from work. Therefore, they are afraid to RTW for fear their stress will increase their risk of cancer recurrence.
A cancer survivor wants to continue working during treatment because she feels working allows her to stay connected to colleagues and prevents her from feeling socially isolated.
An older aged working cancer survivor is concerned that his employer will be less keen to have him back because the temporary replacement worker in his job is younger and is paid at a lower income.
Access to and navigating different systems can delay or impede a person’s ability to RTW. Examples of systems include:
Health care and community (timely access to treatment, symptom management, rehabilitation, provider views on cancer and work)
Financial supports and economic situations (public vs. private insurance)
Legal supports (human rights, employment legislation, collective agreements)
Microsystems (individual’s social, cultural, and family influences)
Scenarios:
A breast cancer survivor wants to delay returning to work until she has reconstructive surgery which is scheduled in 4 months.
A cancer survivor has access to funding for an exercise program through a long-term disability provider to help to restore her physical work ability sooner.
A cancer survivor is worried that if she takes too much time off for treatment, she will not have the legal protection to retain her job.
Worksite factors are unique to the workplace. Examples include:
Physical, psychological, and cognitive job demands
Schedule (part-time vs. full-time, evenings vs. days, work hours)
Employer’s ability and willingness to provide accommodations
Relationship with employers/colleagues (attitudes, dialogue, and support)
Scenarios:
The job is very physically demanding, and the cancer survivor has lost physical conditioning and suffers from fatigue. The employer has allowed her to do lighter duties.
The cancer survivor is currently unable to do full-time work and the employer has allowed for a graduated RTW.
The cancer survivor is concerned that she will not be supported during her RTW because some coworkers do not like her.

sections.title: iCanWork Step 2: Assess function and challenges that impact work

content.text: Assessing function and challenges is one of the most important steps to the return to work (RTW0 process of cancer survivor’s independent of age and clinical factors. (1) It may include understanding work-related abilities, whether an individual is ready for RTW, whether they require more recovery time, and whether a referral to medical, rehabilitation, psychological, and/or worksite support is needed.
There are four types of assessments commonly used together to determine work ability.
Click on the tabs below to learn more about each assessment type.
Cancer Survivor                Self-Assessments
Primary Care               Assessments
Allied Health               Assessments
On-the Job                Assessments
What is a cancer survivor self-assessment?

Cancer Survivor self-assessments are used to evaluate the cancer and treatment impact on an individual’s psycho-social, physical, and cognitive functions. They include self-reports and / or formal and informal screening and assessment tools.
Why must we use these types of assessments?
Cancer survivor self-assessments are valuable both for primary care providers and cancer survivors in a number of ways:
Increase understanding of factors impacting the cancer survivor's ability to work
Use results to inform and focus survivor-provider discussions and direction of care
Cite self-assessment measures to support clinical opinions on insurance and RTW planning forms
Assess readiness for RTW
Who completes them, and when can they be completed?
Primary care providers can complete evaluations through inquiry at scheduled appointment(s) with the cancer survivor
Survivor can complete self-report assessments prior to a scheduled appointment(s)
What are some examples of cancer survivor self-assessments?
Cancer and Work Job Analysis Tool asks cancer survivors to self-rate their physical strength and function, job temperaments, psychological and cognitive demands, and environmental conditions
Click on the image below to access (PDF):

Fatigue Tracking Tool measures fatigue over the day to guide readiness for RTW.(2) Additionally, it can help determine the number of hours for a graduated work simulation and graduated return to work.
Click on the image below to access (PDF):
Cognitive Symptoms at Work Checklist is a modified checklist (3) that measures work-specific cognitive problems for cancer survivors. (4)
Click on the image below to access (online):
Cancer Survivor
Self-Assessments
Primary Care               Assessments
Allied Health                Assessments
On-the Job                Assessments
What is a primary care assessment?

Primary care assessments examine a cancer survivor’s status with respect to the most common side effects of cancer and treatment that impact ability to work including physical, cognitive, and psychological challenges.
Examples of physical challenges ▼
Fatigue
Sleep disturbance
Pain
Nerve damage
Lymphedema
Hot flashes
Breathing difficulties
Nausea
Eating and nutritional challenges
Changes in bowel and bladder function
Visual impairment
Impaired communication abilities
Seizures
Infection risk
Bleeding problems
Changes in skin and nails
Changes in arm, hand, and mobility function
For more information, please see https://www.cancerandwork.ca/healthcare-providers/cancers-impact-on-work/
Examples of cognitive and psychological challenges ▼
Thinking
Memory
Speed of processing
Attention
Anxiety
Depression

Note: At the present, there are no established guidelines for evaluating cancer-related cognitive impairments (CRCI). While neuropsychology is considered the gold standard for assessing cognitive function, in the case of assessment for work purposes, neuropsychology assessments should be work-focused and performed by those familiar with the CRCI literature. Functional assessments can be performed by allied health professionals, such as neurological specialized occupational therapists, and other specialists.
For more information, please see https://www.cancerandwork.ca/healthcare-providers/cancers-impact-on-work/
Why must we use these types of assessments?
Primary care assessments are critical for evaluating an individual’s ability to RTW. More specifically, these assessments can help primary care providers determine:
Possibility of RTW in a particular job/role
Need for additional treatment and interventions prior to returning to work (e.g. referrals to specialists)
Need for accommodations in a particular job or role
Who completes them, and when can they be completed?

The primary care provider completes these assessments. Timely sharing of these assessments helps determine if other professional assessments are needed, supports preparation for a RTW timeline, and prevents undue delay in RTW.

Pan-Canadian Practice Guideline for Screening, Assessment, and Management of Cancer-Related Fatigue in Adults provides a list of pain assessment tools in the public domain that may assist providers in better understanding the impact of pain on a person.

Click on the image below to access (online):

Self-Assessments

Allied Health                Assessments
On-the Job                Assessments
What is an allied health assessment?

Allied health assessments can help provide a supplemental view of the cancer survivor situation and establish their strengths, restrictions, and limitations with respect to their job. Note that these types of assessments may not always be available within the healthcare system but may be accessed through private insurance providers (e.g., short- or long-term disability plan), health care services (e.g., extended health or employee and family assistance programs), and community services (e.g.,  government-funded employment programs.)
Why must we use these types of assessments?

Allied health assessments can further clarify functional challenges and supplement primary care assessments. Additionally, they may provide or guide rehabilitation activities if the individual is not ready to RTW.
Who completes them, and when can they be completed?
Work-focused allied health assessments are often conducted by occupational therapists, neuropsychologists, physiotherapists, psychologists, and vocational rehabilitation counselors.

While early referrals to allied health professionals ensure continuity of service and limit delays in the RTW process, assessments could be carried out when the cancer survivor displays a stable functional presentation, if possible.
What are some examples of allied health assessments?

Examples of allied health assessment and evaluations include functional, physical capacity evaluations, neuropsychological tests, and vocational rehabilitation assessments. More information on professional assessments can be accessed on the Cancer and Work: Professional Assessments webpage.

Self-Assessments
Primary Care               Assessments
Allied Health                Assessments
On-the Job                Assessments
What is an on-the-job assessment?
On-the-job assessments are comprehensive observations and evaluations that provide information to guide an individual’s gradual RTW.
Why must we use these types of assessments?
On-the-job assessments provide a safe and low barrier opportunity for the individual to gradually return to and sustain their ability to work.
Who completes them, and when can they be completed?

If deemed safe by the primary care provider, on-the-job assessments can occur during a graduated RTW trial. In some cases, specialized rehabilitation specialists such as occupational therapists (including physical, psychological and cognitive assessments) or specially trained kinesiologists and physiotherapists can observe and assess the survivor working on the job (often funded by insurance providers).
What are some examples of on-the-job assessments?

Examples of on-the-job assessments include work-focused assessments, working with a colleague (buddy system), gradual return to work trial, and functional capacity evaluations. More information on professional assessments can be accessed on the Cancer and Work: Professional Assessments webpage.

Part of the assessment of a cancer survivor’s functional abilities for working entails comparing current abilities to current job demands (e.g., cognitive, psychological, and physical demands; environmental conditions; and workplace culture in order to identify work-related strengths and challenges.(1) Understanding these considerations may inform the RTW plan and help determine the cancer survivor’s readiness for work.
To gain a better understanding of the cancer survivor’s job demands, primary care providers can:
Obtain or ask the cancer survivor to obtain a job analysis, a job description, or a completed Cancer Work Job Analysis form for employers.
Ask the cancer survivor to conduct their own job analysis by completing the Cancer Work Job Analysis form for survivors.

Discuss job demands (cognitive, psychological, and physical), environmental conditions, and workplace culture. Compare these to the cancer survivor’s work abilities considering their short-, late-, and long-term effects of cancer and its treatment.

Refer or make recommendations to fund allied health providers for formal job analysis assessment, evaluation, and recommendations. Though occupational therapy assessments are not always available within the healthcare system, they may be funded by insurance providers.

pages.title: Learning Check #1
pages.content:
Case Study

Sally is a 58 year old cancer survivor who completed surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy for breast cancer 6 months ago, and is currently awaiting breast reconstruction. She previously worked as a manager of payroll in a large company and has been off work for 18 months receiving long-term disability benefits. The company has informed her that her job is available to her for now.

Sally reports lymphedema which causes her arm to swell and neuropathy in her fingers which causes loss of sensation and pain. Both late effects are causing difficulty in keyboarding. She reports she is also experiencing fatigue, difficulty sleeping, and cognitive challenges.

She reports that her work is stressful particularly related to multitasking and that she is accountable to many staff members. Sally confides that she is fearful that stress is not good for her health. She feels unsure about her ability to work and her readiness to return to work. 

Continue to the next page to answer the learning check questions pertaining to this case.

  • A cancer survivor wants to continue working during treatment because she feels working allows her to stay connected to colleagues and prevents her from feeling socially isolated.
  • An older-aged working cancer survivor is concerned that his employer will be less keen to have him back because the temporary replacement worker in his job is younger and is paid at a lower income.

Access to and navigating different systems can delay or impede a person’s ability to RTW. Examples of systems include:

  • Health care and community (timely access to treatment, symptom management, rehabilitation, provider views on cancer and work)
  • Financial supports and economic situations (public vs. private insurance)
  • Legal supports (human rights, employment legislation, collective agreements)
  • Microsystems (individual’s social, cultural, and family influences)
Scenarios:
  • A breast cancer survivor wants to delay returning to work until she has reconstructive surgery which is scheduled in 4 months.
  • A cancer survivor has access to funding for an exercise program through a long-term disability provider to help to restore her physical work ability sooner.
  • A cancer survivor is worried that if she takes too much time off for treatment, she will not have the legal protection to retain her job.

Worksite factors are unique to the workplace. Examples include:

  • Physical, psychological, and cognitive job demands
  • Schedule (part-time vs. full-time, evenings vs. days, work hours)
  • Employer's availability and willingness to provide accommodations
  • Relationship with employers/colleagues (attitudes, dialogue, and support)
Scenarios:
  • The job is very physically demanding, and the cancer survivor has lost physical conditioning and suffers from fatigue. The employer has allowed her to do lighter duties.
  • The cancer survivor is currently unable to do full-time work and the employer has allowed for a graduated RTW.
  • The cancer survivor is concerned that she will not be supported during her RTW because some coworkers do not like her.

References

  1. Parkinson, M. & Maheu, C. Cancer and Work. Canadian Oncology Nursing Journal / Revue canadienne de soins infirmiers en oncologie 29, 258–266 (2019).

content.text: After exploring the barriers and facilitators to return to work (RTW) (Step 1) and understanding the functional challenges that can impact work ability (Step 2) in comparison to the demands of the job (Step 3), an important role for primary care providers is to address an individual's treatment needs and if indicated, making referrals.
Examples of how to address treatment needs ▼
To help reduce or overcome identified challenges, primary care providers can facilitate:
Timely access to medical treatments and symptom management
Consultation from other services including:
Rehabilitation
Psychological treatment
Pain and symptom management
Vocational rehabilitation
Social work

With respect to post-cancer treatment vocational rehabilitation programs, there have been higher RTW rates within multidisciplinary treatment approaches using vocational counselling, physical activity and psychoeducation.(1)  By developing knowledge of available clinicians and programs, primary care providers can offer, recommend, or refer to services that will support successful reintegration into the workforce post-cancer.
Examples of where services may be accessed ▼
Rehabilitation centres
Hospitals and community health centres
Community centres

Ongoing communication with employers through all stages of recovery is critical to RTW. As the return grows closer, it is crucial that all parties have an understanding of the cancer survivor’s physical, psychological, cognitive, and functional abilities and limitations. This understanding will help the employer and employee collaborate in shared planning to set realistic goals and prepare the workplace. Steps to Communicating with a Survivor’s Employer Employers may request that primary care providers complete a form or provide a letter indicating that the survivor is cleared to RTW and provide a plan. This form or letter needs to include: An itemized list of restrictions and limitations relevant to the job with prompts to consider accommodations as neededRecommendations for reasonable work-site accommodationsIt is ideal to review all recommendations with the cancer survivor prior to submitting forms to the employer. You will also need to obtain written consent from the survivor before providing the employer with any information. Once a form has been sent to the employer, the primary care provider can provide ongoing recommendations as needed. What is an allied health assessment?Allied health assessments can help provide a supplemental view of the cancer survivor situation and establish their strengths, restrictions, and limitations with respect to their job. Note that these types of assessments may not always be available within the healthcare system but may be accessed through private insurance providers (e.g., short- or long-term disability plan), health care services (e.g., extended health or employee and family assistance programs), and community services (e.g.,  government-funded employment programs.)Why must we use these types of assessments?Allied health assessments can further clarify functional challenges and supplement primary care assessments. Additionally, they may provide or guide rehabilitation activities if the individual is not ready to RTW. Who completes them, and when can they be completed?Work-focused allied health assessments are often conducted by occupational therapists, neuropsychologists, physiotherapists, psychologists, and vocational rehabilitation counselors. While early referrals to allied health professionals ensure continuity of service and limit delays in the RTW process, assessments could be carried out when the cancer survivor displays a stable functional presentation, if possible.What are some examples of allied health assessments?Examples of allied health assessment and evaluations include functional, physical capacity evaluations, neuropsychological tests, and vocational rehabilitation assessments. More information on professional assessments can be accessed on the Cancer and Work: Professional Assessments webpage.

What is an on-the-job assessment?On-the-job assessments are comprehensive observations and evaluations that provide information to guide an individual’s gradual RTW.Why must we use these types of assessments?On-the-job assessments provide a safe and low barrier opportunity for the individual to gradually return to and sustain their ability to work.Who completes them, and when can they be completed?If deemed safe by the primary care provider, on-the-job assessments can occur during a graduated RTW trial. In some cases, specialized rehabilitation specialists such as occupational therapists (including physical, psychological and cognitive assessments) or specially trained kinesiologists and physiotherapists can observe and assess the survivor working on the job (often funded by insurance providers).What are some examples of on-the-job assessments?Examples of on-the-job assessments include work-focused assessments, working with a colleague (buddy system), gradual return to work trial, and functional capacity evaluations. More information on professional assessments can be accessed on the Cancer and Work: Professional Assessments webpage.

Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is reported as one of the most common and distressing side effects of cancer and treatment, causing greater interference with daily life than any other symptom.(7) Additionally, it impacts personal, social, work roles and it can have a profound negative impact on overall quality of life. Because its etiology is not well understood, it is often unrecognized and difficult to manage. Better management of CRF is needed in view of its strong association with return to work (RTW).IdentifyScreening for fatigue occurs periodically. Assessments (e.g., Edmonton Symptom Assessment System Revised, [ESAS-r]) and physical exams may be accompanied by a focused or comprehensive assessment of fatigue, if indicated. (8)TreatTo treat and educate cancer survivors on how to manage fatigue, primary care providers can:Integrate sleep education, problem-solving skills, stress management, and psychological counselling into psychoeducational interventions and multi-component cognitive behavioural therapy approaches.Promote and individualize a gradual and moderate (55-75%) exercise program with a variety of options (i.e. cardiovascular, flexibility, and strength training), as appropriate.Provide ongoing assessment of possible causal factors to determine whether additional targeted interventions are required (sleep, depression).(8)ReferIf indicated, refer to psychological/counselling, occupational therapy, and oncology exercise specialists, or fatigue management programs, as required.

Cognitive function refers to mental processes involved in the acquisition of knowledge, manipulation of information and reasoning. Cognitive function includes perception, attention, learning, memory, executive function, and language. When a problem arises in cognitive function due to cancer and/or its treatment, it is called cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) and can be a barrier to successful return to work (RTW) for cancer survivors. These problems are more severe and more common in patients with cancers that directly involve the central nervous system (CNS), such as a primary brain tumour(11) but are also seen in 25% of patients treated for non-CNS  tumours.(12-14)IdentifyFunctional assessments can be performed by occupational therapists,  speech-language pathologists, vocational rehabilitation counselors, and more specialized assessments such as for driving can be done through driving assessment and  rehabilitation centres.Neuropsychology assessments should be work-focused and done by those familiar with the CRCI literature.To support assessments for CRCI, primary care providers can:Screen for cognitive challenges that might impact work ability (e.g. cognitive symptoms at work  self report tool).Provide ongoing assessment of possible causal factors such as: sleep problems (e.g., apnea, severe insomnia), anxiety or depression, nutritional deficiencies (e.g., low B12, anemia), and thyroid abnormalities to determine whether additional targeted interventions are required. General (non work-focused) exercise studies have shown that participating in an exercise program can lead to reduced time to return to work (RTW), increased hours of work, improved sustained work outcomes (22), improved productivity (23), improved perceived ability to work, and improved quality of life. (24) There is a strong track record in rehabilitation to provide for work hardening and work conditioning.  Exercise Guidelines for Cancer Survivors: Consensus Statement from International Multidisciplinary Roundtable (25) concludes “that exercise training and testing were generally safe for cancer survivors and that every survivor should “avoid inactivity.” As well, specific doses of aerobic, combined aerobic plus resistance training, and/ or resistance training can improve common cancer-related health outcomes including anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, physical functioning, and health-related quality of life.(17-19) Implications for other outcomes, such as peripheral neuropathy and cognitive functioning, remain uncertain. Pain is not experienced in isolation, and is usually accompanied by other symptoms, such as sleep disturbance and mood disorders, and potential negative impact on social consequences, work and finances. It is important that all symptoms are managed concurrently.From a functional perspective, long-term effects such as chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy and lymphedema can negatively impact a cancer survivor’s ability to complete even basic work tasks, such as balance and walking, handling objects and hand dexterity, and communication. It is critical that survivors and their employers are aware of the individual’s symptoms, needs, and functional status in order to accommodate and plan for a successful return to work (RTW) program.TreatTo treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage pain, discomfort, sensory changes, and edema, primary care providers can:Consider both non-pharmaceutical  and pharmaceutical approaches to treatment of pain.Discuss  risks,  limitations, and potential  accommodations to address the impact of neuropathy and pain (i.e. handrails, skid-free flooring, reduced speed expectations, limiting walking and standing, adapted writing utensils, modified keyboards, voice-activated software, more frequent sensory breaks to complete therapeutic programming and recover from the effects of pain).Utilize a tailored approach to making recommendations for  lymphedema management at work, with consideration of  individualized symptoms and experiences, the work role, and the nature and location of the edema. Adolescents and Young Adults (AYA) population includes individuals between the ages of 15 and 39. In many cases, the cancer treatment for AYAs can be more aggressive compared to older survivors, (35) with one-third of AYAs experiencing later-onset sequelae of cancer. The most common risk of late effects from cancer and treatment include metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, chronic heart failure, obesity and neurocognitive challenges resulting in loss of productivity (36) and work capabilities. (37,38) AYAs report concentration problems, and the physical impacts of their treatment including fatigue as their greatest challenge with regards to the reintegration of school and work. (39) Hence the importance of providing specific AYA return to work (RTW) support along with vocational counselling.TreatTo treat, advise, and educate AYA cancer survivors on successful RTW, primary care providers can:Provide ongoing screening of distress and treat if indicated. Advise to engage, re-access, or continue with vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling, and social work support to address job loss, to seek alternative work (if needed), and address underemployment (for employed individuals with ongoing disability challenges or new onset of late-effects). Advise and educate AYA cancer survivors to engage in career exploration by undertaking practical, work-related life experiences (e.g., exploring recreational interests, volunteering, taking on part-time work roles). This may help them develop and explore vocational interests, aptitudes, and abilities. Encourage school-aged survivors and/or families to advocate with the schools and hospitals for up-to-date neuropsychological assessment before they graduate. This can help guide career selection, choice of education and vocational training, and accommodations needed for work.Encourage AYAs to view engagement with supports such as counselling, employment counselling services, vocational rehabilitation as  being resourceful and not a challenge to independence.ReferTo address distress, if indicated, provide timely referral to psychosocial support such as counselling, social work, and, if indicated, psychiatry. Given that AYA are often in a stage of identity formation and at higher risk for unemployment, refer to tailored vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling programs, and therapeutic rehabilitation.If navigating government services is too challenging, encourage the AYA survivor to seek out  support from family members, social workers, and vocational rehabilitation specialists to facilitate connections and support navigating systems.See employment programs listed on the Cancer and Work website for a list of Cancer specific and general vocational rehabilitation programs in Canada. Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is reported as one of the most common and distressing side effects of cancer and treatment, causing greater interference with daily life than any other symptom.(7) Additionally, it impacts personal, social, work roles and it can have a profound negative impact on overall quality of life. Because its etiology is not well understood, it is often unrecognized and difficult to manage. Better management of CRF is needed in view of its strong association with return to work (RTW).
Identify

Screening for fatigue occurs periodically. Assessments (e.g., Edmonton Symptom Assessment System Revised, [ESAS-r]) and physical exams may be accompanied by a focused or comprehensive assessment of fatigue, if indicated. (8)
Treat
To treat and educate cancer survivors on how to manage fatigue, primary care providers can:
Integrate sleep education, problem-solving skills, stress management, and psychological counselling into psychoeducational interventions and multi-component cognitive behavioural therapy approaches.
Promote and individualize a gradual and moderate (55-75%) exercise program with a variety of options (i.e. cardiovascular, flexibility, and strength training), as appropriate.
Provide ongoing assessment of possible causal factors to determine whether additional targeted interventions are required (sleep, depression).(8)
Refer
If indicated, refer to psychological/counselling, occupational therapy, and oncology exercise specialists, or fatigue management programs, as required.

Cognitive function refers to mental processes involved in the acquisition of knowledge, manipulation of information and reasoning. Cognitive function includes perception, attention, learning, memory, executive function, and language. When a problem arises in cognitive function due to cancer and/or its treatment, it is called cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) and can be a barrier to successful return to work (RTW) for cancer survivors. These problems are more severe and more common in patients with cancers that directly involve the central nervous system (CNS), such as a primary brain tumour(11) but are also seen in 25% of patients treated for non-CNS  tumours.(12-14)
Identify

Functional assessments can be performed by occupational therapists,  speech-language pathologists, vocational rehabilitation counselors, and more specialized assessments such as for driving can be done through driving assessment and  rehabilitation centres.
Neuropsychology assessments should be work-focused and done by those familiar with the CRCI literature.
To support assessments for CRCI, primary care providers can:
Screen for cognitive challenges that might impact work ability (e.g. cognitive symptoms at work  self report tool).

Provide ongoing assessment of possible causal factors such as: sleep problems (e.g., apnea, severe insomnia), anxiety or depression, nutritional deficiencies (e.g., low B12, anemia), and thyroid abnormalities to determine whether additional targeted interventions are required.

Monitor for non-cancer medical conditions which can independently be associated with cognitive impairment (e.g., diabetes, cerebral vascular disease, high blood pressure) as well as for neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., vascular dementia or Azheimer’s disease) should individuals report further decline in cognitive domains after treatment is complete.
Treat
To treat and educate cancer survivors on causal factors and conditions contributing to cognitive impairment, primary care providers can:
Review medications, dosing, and time when taken regularly, especially if excessive daytime sleepiness is reported.
Refer
As needed, refer to neuropsychology, occupational therapy, and speech pathology to teach compensatory strategies and advise on adaptive aids to improve functioning at work.
Refer to Cancer Center and Community (e.g. Wellspring Canada) for CRCI or Brain Fog Programs, as required.
Refer to public health brain injury rehabilitation services to obtain occupational therapy, physical therapy, and speech pathology for CNS tumours, as required.

While currently in Canada there are very few specialists in neuropsychologists and occupational therapists specialized in oncology, private insurers are increasingly open to funding neurocognitive and work-focused occupational therapy assessments.

Challenges with sleep  can contribute to fatigue and can be a source of concern for cancer survivors with respect to returning to work. Studies indicate that although individuals perceive the inability to sleep as significant and disruptive, they are often reluctant to report these issues. Therefore, sleep may require more attention from health professionals.
Identify
Assess for symptoms of sleep apnea or restless leg disorders.

As recommended by the Pan-Canadian Practice Guideline for Prevention, Screening, Assessment and Treatment of Sleep Disturbances in Adults with Cancer2, screen for sleep disturbances using general medical/psychiatric questionnaires, such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) or other sleepiness assessment. In addition, survivors should be asked to keep a two-week log of their sleeping patterns.
In addition, survivors can be asked to keep a two-week log of their sleeping patterns.
Treat
To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage sleep disturbances, primary care providers can:
Review sleep hygiene.

Support access to sleep-focused cognitive behavioural therapy programs as indicated. These programs promote improved sleep-onset latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, and time in bed. Such programs include:
Stimulus control instructions
Sleep education
Sleep restriction
Proper sleep hygiene

Assess possible causal factors of disruptions in sleep-wake patterns to determine whether other targeted interventions for insomnia disorders (e.g., counselling, medical management, or specialist medical interventions) are required. (20)
Refer
Refer to counselling, medical management or specialist medical interventions for insomnia disorders, as required.

General (non work-focused) exercise studies have shown that participating in an exercise program can lead to reduced time to return to work (RTW), increased hours of work, improved sustained work outcomes (22), improved productivity (23), improved perceived ability to work, and improved quality of life. (24) There is a strong track record in rehabilitation to provide for work hardening and work conditioning.

Exercise Guidelines for Cancer Survivors: Consensus Statement from International Multidisciplinary Roundtable (25) concludes “that exercise training and testing were generally safe for cancer survivors and that every survivor should “avoid inactivity.” As well, specific doses of aerobic, combined aerobic plus resistance training, and/ or resistance training can improve common cancer-related health outcomes including anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, physical functioning, and health-related quality of life.(17-19) Implications for other outcomes, such as peripheral neuropathy and cognitive functioning, remain uncertain.
Treat
To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage physical activity, primary care providers can:

Advise that intensity of physical activity be gradually increased, as tolerated, for a minimum goal of 30 minutes of exercise daily, 5 days per week.(30) Prescribed exercise should be tailored to the survivor’s care needs (i.e. disease site and stage, planned treatments, current fitness level, past and present exercise habits and preferences).
Promote a combination of aerobic exercises, strength training, and flexibility training, as appropriate.
Consider special needs of cancer survivors related to healthy diet recommendations (e.g. ostomy management, swallowing difficulties, drug interactions).
Refer

Refer to registered exercise professionals, kinesiologists, physiotherapists, physiologists, or occupational therapists(26) for tailored, work-focused or work-hardening programs, or for general  non-work exercise programs.
Refer to the Canada Food Guide for healthy diet recommendations.
Refer to a registered dietician to facilitate the adoption of healthy lifestyle management behaviours.

Pain is not experienced in isolation, and is usually accompanied by other symptoms, such as sleep disturbance and mood disorders, and potential negative impact on social consequences, work and finances. It is important that all symptoms are managed concurrently.

From a functional perspective, long-term effects such as chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy and lymphedema can negatively impact a cancer survivor’s ability to complete even basic work tasks, such as balance and walking, handling objects and hand dexterity, and communication. It is critical that survivors and their employers are aware of the individual’s symptoms, needs, and functional status in order to accommodate and plan for a successful return to work (RTW) program.
Treat
To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage pain, discomfort, sensory changes, and edema, primary care providers can:
Consider both non-pharmaceutical  and pharmaceutical approaches to treatment of pain.

Discuss  risks,  limitations, and potential  accommodations to address the impact of neuropathy and pain (i.e. handrails, skid-free flooring, reduced speed expectations, limiting walking and standing, adapted writing utensils, modified keyboards, voice-activated software, more frequent sensory breaks to complete therapeutic programming and recover from the effects of pain).

Utilize a tailored approach to making recommendations for  lymphedema management at work, with consideration of  individualized symptoms and experiences, the work role, and the nature and location of the edema.
Prescribe or consult with rehabilitation services and/or a certified lymphedema therapist regarding compression and garments for lymphedema.
Refer
Referral to occupational therapy, physiotherapy, vocational rehabilitation, and disability management may be indicated to address pain and CIPN and to  address pain-related considerations at work.

Adolescents and Young Adults (AYA) population includes individuals between the ages of 15 and 39. In many cases, the cancer treatment for AYAs can be more aggressive compared to older survivors, (35) with one-third of AYAs experiencing later-onset sequelae of cancer. The most common risk of late effects from cancer and treatment include metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, chronic heart failure, obesity and neurocognitive challenges resulting in loss of productivity (36) and work capabilities. (37,38) AYAs report concentration problems, and the physical impacts of their treatment including fatigue as their greatest challenge with regards to the reintegration of school and work. (39) Hence the importance of providing specific AYA return to work (RTW) support along with vocational counselling.
Treat
To treat, advise, and educate AYA cancer survivors on successful RTW, primary care providers can:
Provide ongoing screening of distress and treat if indicated.

Advise to engage, re-access, or continue with vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling, and social work support to address job loss, to seek alternative work (if needed), and address underemployment (for employed individuals with ongoing disability challenges or new onset of late-effects).

Advise and educate AYA cancer survivors to engage in career exploration by undertaking practical, work-related life experiences (e.g., exploring recreational interests, volunteering, taking on part-time work roles). This may help them develop and explore vocational interests, aptitudes, and abilities.

Encourage school-aged survivors and/or families to advocate with the schools and hospitals for up-to-date neuropsychological assessment before they graduate. This can help guide career selection, choice of education and vocational training, and accommodations needed for work.
Encourage AYAs to view engagement with supports such as counselling, employment counselling services, vocational rehabilitation as  being resourceful and not a challenge to independence.
Refer
To address distress, if indicated, provide timely referral to psychosocial support such as counselling, social work, and, if indicated, psychiatry.

Given that AYA are often in a stage of identity formation and at higher risk for unemployment, refer to tailored vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling programs, and therapeutic rehabilitation.

If navigating government services is too challenging, encourage the AYA survivor to seek out  support from family members, social workers, and vocational rehabilitation specialists to facilitate connections and support navigating systems.
See employment programs listed on the Cancer and Work website for a list of Cancer specific and general vocational rehabilitation programs in Canada.
Tips for communicating with adolescents and young adults:(39)
Image text ▼
Ask about returning to work or school

Before her cancer diagnosis, Sara had a busy career. She took time off during her treatment and has been working part-time for the last few months. She has been struggling with her finances and would like to return to work full-time, but she is experiencing some challenges at work related to her ability to concentrate. Sara is wondering if she will ever be able to return to full-time work, and what she needs to think about in making this decision.
Sara [speaking to her healthcare provider]:
“How do I know when I’m ready?
How do I return to school, and who do I talk to, to get set up?
I have some limitations at work. Still don’t know how to deal with it…
What are my employee rights? How long can an accommodation plan be in place?”
Questions to ask

Recovery and adjusting to life post-treatment can be challenging. Patients often reintegrate back to work and school at their own pace. Have you thought about or started the process of going back to work or school?
What are your biggest concerns about returning to work or school?
