Cognitive function refers to mental processes involved in the acquisition of knowledge, manipulation of information and reasoning. Cognitive function includes perception, attention, learning, memory, executive function, and language. When a problem arises in cognitive function due to cancer and/or its treatment, it is called cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI)Symptoms of CRCI commonly include problems with focusing attention and sustaining concentration, multi-tasking, learning and memory recall, word-finding and processing speed and can be a barrier to successful return to work (RTW) for cancer survivors. These problems are more severe and more common in patients with cancers that directly involve the central nervous system (CNS), such as a primary brain tumour11 but are also seen in 25% of patients treated for non-CNS tomours.12-14

Identify

Functional assessments can be performed by occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists, vocational rehabilitation counsellors. More specialized assessments such as for driving can be done through driving assessment and rehabilitation centres.

Neuropsychology assessments should be work-focused and done by those familiar with the CRCI literature.

To support assessments for CRCI, primary care providers can:

  • Screen for cognitive challenges that might impact work ability (e.g. cognitive symptoms at work self report tool).
  • Provide ongoing assessment of possible causal factors such as: sleep problems (e.g., apnea, severe insomnia), anxiety or depression, nutritional deficiencies (e.g., low B12, anemia), and thyroid abnormalities to determine whether additional targeted interventions are required.
  • Monitor for non-cancer medical conditions which can independently be associated with cognitive impairment (e.g., diabetes, cerebral vascular disease, high blood pressure) as well as for neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., vascular dementia or Azheimer’s disease) should individuals report further decline in cognitive domains after treatment is complete.
Treat

To treat and educate cancer survivors on causal factors and conditions contributing to cognitive impairment, primary care providers can:

  • Review medications, dosing, and time when taken regularly, especially if excessive daytime sleepiness is reported.
Refer

As needed, refer to neuropsychology, occupational therapy, and speech pathology to teach compensatory strategies and advise on adaptive aids to improve functioning at work.

Refer to Cancer Center and Community (e.g. Wellspring Canada) for CRCI or Brain Fog Programs, as required.

Refer to public health brain injury rehabilitation services to obtain occupational therapy, physical therapy, and speech pathology for CNS tumours, as required.

While currently in Canada there are very few specialists in neuropsychologists and occupational therapists specialized in oncology, private insurers are increasingly open to funding neurocognitive and work-focused occupational therapy assessments.

Clinical Tip

A more functional and targeted approach is to combine a neurocognitive-focused occupational therapy assessment with a work site assessment to integrate the context of work. Ideally, the assessment would be combined with cognitive rehabilitation and/or psycho-educational counselling to guide recommendations for accommodations and liaise with the employer.

Challenges with sleep can contribute to fatigue and can be a source of concern for cancer survivors with respect to returning to work. Studies indicate that although individuals perceive the inability to sleep as significant and disruptive, they are often reluctant to report these issues. Therefore, sleep may require more attention from health professionals.

Identify

Assess for symptoms of sleep apnea or restless leg disorders.

As recommended by the Pan-Canadian Practice Guideline for Prevention, Screening, Assessment and Treatment of Sleep Disturbances in Adults with Cancer20, screen for sleep disturbances using general medical/psychiatric questionnaires, such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) or other sleepiness assessment20.

In addition, survivors should be asked to keep a two-week log of their sleeping patterns.

Treat

To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage sleep disturbances, primary care providers can:

  • Review sleep hygiene.
  • Support access to sleep-focused cognitive behavioural therapy programs as indicated. These programs promote improved sleep-onset latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, and time in bed. Such programs include:
    • Stimulus control instructions
    • Sleep education
    • Sleep restriction
    • Proper sleep hygiene
  • Assess possible causal factors of disruptions in sleep-wake patterns to determine whether other targeted interventions for insomnia disorders (e.g., counselling, medical management, or specialist medical interventions) are required.20
Refer

Refer to counselling, medical management or specialist medical interventions for insomnia disorders, as required.

Resources

Oncology Nursing Forum: Sleep-Wake Disturbances in Adults with Cancer Part II: Evaluating the Evidence for Clinical Decision Making

American Society of Clinical Oncology: Clinical Practice Survivorship Guidelines, Endorsements and Adaptations

Pan-Canadian Practice Guidelines: Prevention, Screening, Assessment and Treatment of Sleep Disturbances in Adults with Cancer

General (non work-focused) exercise studies have shown that participating in an exercise program can result in lead to reduced time to return to work (RTW), increased hours of work, improved sustained work outcomes,22 improved productivity,23 improved perceived ability to work, and improved quality of life.24 To date, very few exercise trials have been tailored to the specific demands of the cancer survivor’s job, making it a work-focused intervention. There is a strong track record in rehabilitation to provide for work hardening and work conditioning.

Exercise Guidelines for Cancer Survivors: Consensus Statement from International Multidisciplinary Roundtable25 concludes “that exercise training and testing were generally safe for cancer survivors and that every survivor should “avoid inactivity.” As well, specific doses of aerobic, combined aerobic plus resistance training, and/ or resistance training can improve common cancer-related health outcomes including anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, physical functioning, and health-related quality of life.17, 18, 19 Implications for other outcomes, such as peripheral neuropathy and cognitive functioning, remain uncertain.

Treat

To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage physical activity, primary care providers can:

  • Advise that intensity of physical activity be gradually increased, as tolerated, for a minimum goal of 30 minutes of exercise daily, 5 days per week.30 Prescribed exercise should be tailored to the survivor’s care needs (i.e. disease site and stage, planned treatments, current fitness level, past and present exercise habits and preferences).
  • Promote a combination of aerobic exercises, strength training, and flexibility training, as appropriate.
  • Consider special needs of cancer survivors related to healthy diet recommendations (e.g. ostomy management, swallowing difficulties, drug interactions).
Refer

Refer to registered exercise professionals, kinesiologists, physiotherapists, physiologists, or occupational therapists26 for tailored, work-focused or work hardening programsWork hardening programs can improve the chances of expediting RTW and may be funded by insurance providers and be facilitated with the recommendation of a primary care provider or for general non-work exercise programs.

Refer to the Canada Food Guide for healthy diet recommendations.

Refer to a registered dietician to facilitate the adoption of healthy lifestyle management behaviours.

Resources

Pan-Canadian Guidance: Organization and Structure of Survivorship Services and Psychosocial-Supportive Care Best Practices for Adult Cancer Survivors

Current Oncology: Exercise for people with cancer: a clinical practice guideline

Cancer Care Ontario: A Quality Initiative of the Program in Evidence-Based Care (PEBC): Exercise for People with Cancer

American Cancer Society: Exercise is medicine in oncology: Engaging clinicians to help patients move through cancer

Pain is not experienced in isolation, and is usually accompanied by other symptoms, such as sleep disturbance and mood disorders, and potential negative impact on social consequences, work and finances. It is important that all symptoms are managed concurrently.

From a functional perspective, long-term effects such as chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathyChemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CINP) is an injury or degeneration of the peripheral nerve fibers (motor, sensory, autonomic) caused by certain neurotoxic systemic therapy agents.34 Symptoms usually start in the fingers and toes and spread proximally in a glove and stocking distribution. and lymphedemaLymphedema can develop from cancer-related and treatment-related factors such as with surgical intervention, lymph node dissections, and radiation therapy. Cancer-related lymphedema is considered a lifelong, chronic and episodic condition that manifests through swelling of an impacted area of the body, depending on where the lymph nodes and lymphatic system have experienced trauma and/or damage. can negatively impact a cancer survivor’s ability to complete even basic work tasks, such as balance and walking, handling objects and hand dexterity, and communication. It is critical that survivors and their employers are aware of the individual’s symptoms, needs, and functional status in order to accommodate and plan for a successful return to work (RTW) program.

Treat

To treat, support, and educate cancer survivors on how to manage pain, discomfort, sensory changes, and edema, primary care providers can:

  • Consider both non-pharmiceutical and pharmaceutical approaches to treatment of pain.
  • Discuss risks, limitations, and accommodations resulting from neuropathy and pain (i.e. handrails, skid-free flooring, reduced speed expectations, limiting walking and standing, adapted writing utensils, modified keyboards, voice-activated software, more frequent sensory breaks to complete therapeutic programming and recover from the effects of pain).
  • Utilize a tailored approach to making recommendations for lymphedema management at work, with consideration of individualized symptoms and experiences, the work role, and the nature and location of the edema.
  • Prescribe or consult with rehabilitation services and/or a certified lymphedema therapist regarding compression and garments for lymphedema.
Refer

Referral to occupational therapy, physiotherapy, vocational rehabilitation, and disability management may be indicated to address pain and CIPN and to address pain-related considerations at work.

Clinical Tip

In most cases of neuropathy, the bulk of recovery comes within the first 6 months post-treatment, but there can be residual effects and full recovery may take years post-treatment.

Resources

Pain Medicine: Chronic Pain in the Cancer Survivor: A New Frontier

Adolescents and Young Adults (AYA) population includes individuals between the ages of 15 and 39. In many cases, the cancer treatment for AYAs can be more aggressive compared to older survivors,35 with one-third of AYAs experiencing later-onset sequelae of cancer. The most common risk of late effects from cancer and treatment include metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, chronic heart failure, obesity and neurocognitive challenges resulting in loss of productivity36 and work capabilities.37, 38 AYAs report concentration problems, and the physical impacts of their treatment including fatigue as their greatest challenge with regards to the reintegration of school and work39. Hence the importance of providing specific AYA return to work (RTW) support along with vocational counselling.

Treat

To treat, advise, and educate AYA cancer survivors on successful RTW, primary care providers can:

  • Provide ongoing screening of distress and treat, if indicated.
  • Advise to engage, re-access, or continue with vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling, and social work support to address job loss, to seek alternative work (if needed), and to address underemployment (for employed individuals with ongoing disability challenges or new onset of late-effects).

Advise and educate AYA cancer survivors to engage in career exploration by undertaking practical, work-related life experiences (e.g., exploring recreational interests, volunteering, taking on part-time work roles). This may help them develop and explore vocational interests, aptitudes, and abilities.

Encourage school-aged survivors and/or families to advocate with the schools and hospitals for up-to-date neuropsychological assessment before they graduate. This can help guide career selection, choice of education and vocational training, and accommodations needed for work.

Encourage AYAs to view engagement with supports such as counselling, employment counselling services, vocational rehabilitation as being resourceful and not a challenge to independence.

Refer

To address distress, if indicated, provide timely referral to psychosocial support such as counselling, social work, and, if indicated, psychiatry.

Given that AYA are often in a stage of identity formation and at higher risk for unemployment, refer to tailored vocational rehabilitation, employment counselling programs, and therapeutic rehabilitation.

If navigating government services is too challenging, encourage the AYA survivor to seek out support from family members, social workers, and vocational rehabilitation specialists to facilitate connections and support navigating systems.

See employment programs listed on the Cancer and Work website for a list of Cancer specific and general vocational rehabilitation programs in Canada.

Tips for communicating with adolescents and young adults:39

Image text ▼

Ask about returning to work or school

Before her cancer diagnosis, Sara had a busy career. She took time off during her treatment and has been working part-time for the last few months. She has been struggling with her finances and would like to RTW full-time, but she is experiencing some challenges at work related to her ability to concentrate. Sara is wondering if she will ever be able to return to full-time work, and what she needs to think about in making this decision.

Sara [speaking to her healthcare provider]:

“How do I know when I’m ready?
How do I return to school, and who do I talk to, to get set up?
I have some limitations at work. Still don’t know how to deal with it…
What are my employee rights? How long can an accommodation plan be in place?”

Questions to ask:

  • Recovery and adjusting to life post-treatment can be challenging. Patients often reintegrate back to work and school at their own pace. Have you thought about or started the process of going back to work or school?
  • What are your biggest concerns about returning to work or school?
  • Now that you are back at work or school, how is that going for you?

pages.title: Learning Check #2
pages.content:
Case Study

Sally is a 58 year old cancer survivor who completed surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy for breast cancer 6 months ago, and is currently awaiting breast reconstruction. She previously worked as a manager of payroll in a large company and has been off work for 18 months receiving long-term disability benefits. The company has informed her that her job is available to her for now.

Sally reports lymphedema which causes her arm to swell and neuropathy in her fingers which causes loss of sensation and pain. Both late effects are causing difficulty in keyboarding. She reports she is also experiencing fatigue, difficulty sleeping and has cognitive challenges. 

She reports that her work is stressful particularly related to multitasking and that she is accountable to many staff members. Sally confides that she is fearful that stress is not good for her health. She feels unsure about her ability to work and her readiness to return to work.

Continue to the next page to answer the learning check questions pertaining to this case.
Total number of questions: 3

pages.title: iCanWork Step 4: Identify, Treat, and Refer to Support
pages.content:
After exploring the barriers and facilitators to return to work (RTW) (Step 1) and understanding the functional challenges that can impact work ability (Step 2) in comparison to the demands of the job (Step 3), an important role for primary care providers is to address an individual's treatment needs and if indicated, make referrals. 

Examples of how to address treatment needs ▼

To help reduce or overcome identified challenges, primary care providers can facilitate:

  • Timely access to medical treatments and symptom management
  • Consultation from other services including:
    • Rehabilitation
    • Psychological treatment
    • Pain and symptom management
    • Vocational rehabilitation
    • Social work

With respect to post-cancer treatment vocational rehabilitation programs, there have been higher RTW rates within multidisciplinary treatment approaches using vocational counselling, physical activity and psychoeducation.1 By developing knowledge of available clinicians and programs, primary care providers can offer, recommend, or refer to services that will support successful reintegration into the workforce post-cancer.

Examples of where services may be accessed ▼

  • Rehabilitation centres
  • Hospitals and community health centres
  • Community centres
  • Private services
  • Oncology sites
  • Advocacy services
Overview of Recommended Services Based on RTW Status

Click on the cards below to reveal the services from which individuals of each RTW status may benefit

Individuals returning to their former job/workplace

  • Diagnostic and treatment services
  • Rehabilitation technology
  • Job accommodation services3

Individuals looking for work

  • Vocational training
  • Job-seeking skills
  • Job placement services3

Individuals seeking a change in job/workplace

  • Career exploration and assessment
  • Informational interviewing
  • Volunteering and part-time work
  • Engaging in daily tasks that explore their vocational interests
  • Vocational rehabilitation support, if needed

References

  2. Duijts SF, van Egmond MP, Spelten E, van Muijen P, Anema JR, van der Beek AJ. Physical and psychosocial problems in cancer survivors beyond return to work: a systematic review. Psychooncology. 2014;23(5):481-492.

pages.title: iCanWork Step 5: Encourage Survivors to Take Control
pages.content:
Research suggests that when cancer survivors play an active role in their return to work (RTW), they have better work ability outcomes.1 By encouraging cancer survivors to actively self-educate and participate in their work focused rehabilitation, you will help them to:2

  • Develop a better understanding of their challenges and opportunities
  • Develop resiliency skills
  • Learn how to optimize their own health and well-being
  • Facilitate their RTW

The Role of Primary Care

Encourage survivors to explore and access services that are available through:

  • Cancer centres, other health care organizations, or community agencies
  • Government departments or government-funded agencies
  • Private sector services through insurance, employee and family assistance, extended health, or self-pay
  • Online groups or resources
  • Emotional support available in-person, virtually, or by phone

Resources

    • To find out about resources in their community, survivors can consult the Canadian Cancer Society’s Community Locator
    • Vocational rehabilitation and employment resources (cancer and general): Employment and vocational rehabilitation support
    • Non-profit human rights organizations and legal organizations

Non-cancer specific resources that target individuals with health conditions as a result of cancer and treatments (e.g. brain injury, psychological challenges, pain, amputations, sleep challenges, etc.) may be useful to support the RTW process.

pages.title: Summary of Key Points
pages.content:
Primary care providers can support cancer survivors to address challenges related to return to work by:
  • Providing referrals to allied health specialists for medical treatments and symptom management
  • Considering referrals or making recommendations to access resources within the healthcare system, private healthcare and the community to address the challenges that impact work
  • Encouraging cancer survivors to be resourceful in researching and accessing care, engaging in self self-management strategies, and educating themselves on the return to work process

lessons.title: LESSON 4 | RETURN TO WORK: TRANSITIONING TO THE WORKPLACE

sections.title: iCanWork Step 6: Identify and foster workplace supports

content.text: Helping identify and foster workplace supports for cancer survivors has both benefits and challenges:
To identify and foster workplace supports, primary care providers can:

Provide a letter, fill out forms, or directly communicate with the workplace in a timely manner, with the cancer survivor’s consent, regarding the individual’s fitness and readiness for return to work (RTW)
Encourage cancer survivors to discuss and determine how best to address RTW with their employer
Inquire about  the level of support an employer is able and ready to provide, and tailor RTW plan accordingly
Examples of questions you can ask ▼
What supports and accommodations are routinely offered? What have others received post-illness and/or injury?
What accommodation is the employer able or willing to provide? (i.e. graduated return to work, flexible hours, working from home)
What timeline is the employer willing to accept for a graduate RTW?
Refer to counselling or social work services to address the cancer survivor’s challenges with setting boundaries and assertiveness
Refer to vocational rehabilitation, social work, or counselling services if the cancer survivor is reluctant to speak to the employer
Share resources to support survivors' understanding of how to exercise their power of disclosure

If the employer is reluctant to provide needed accommodations,  encourage the cancer survivor to review legal answers or consult their local human rights organization on employers' rights to medical information

sections.title: iCanWork Step 7: Contribute to the development of a return to work plan

content.text: Return to work (RTW) plans are co-developed by an employer and cancer survivor with input from other parties involved in the RTW process (i.e. healthcare providers). Plans should be individualized and flexible to meet each survivor’s unique needs and the employer’s ability to provide accommodations (1,2).

sections.title: iCanWork Step 8: Prepare survivors for an imminent return to work

content.text: While off work, cancer survivors may have lost work-conditioning and work habits. Timely work-focused advice on fatigue, sleep and symptom management, and energy allocation can help cancer survivors’ transition back to work.
In preparation for returning to work, primary care providers can encourage survivors to:
Consider and practice work routines
E.g. restructuring wake times to mirror work schedules
Attempt work simulations
E.g. doing light housekeeping if safe and/or working on the computer

Seek help with transportation to work for those with limited energy or no longer able to drive

E.g. communicate needs with those at the workplace.

pages.title: iCanWork Step 6: Identify and Foster Workplace Supports
pages.content:
The Role of Primary Care

Primary care providers play a pivotal role in encouraging cancer survivors to stay in contact with those at their workplace. Staying in contact is particularly important when returning to a former position to help maintain positive relationships which foster a supportive environment while transitioning back into the workforce. This can be achieved by maintaining ongoing positive communication with management and colleagues.1–7

Helping identify and foster of workplace supports for cancer survivors has both benefits and challenges:
Benefits Challenges
● Ongoing and early discussion about RTW can encourage the employer to keep a job available to the cancer survivor. ● In some cases, survivors who stay in contact with colleagues may experience pressure to RTW before they are ready.4
● Advance notice about RTW dates offers employers the necessary time to prepare and arrange for any accommodations. ● Cancer survivors may be reluctant to stay in contact with those at work because they may have concerns about disclosing their cancer.
● Supportive workplace relationships with colleagues have been found to be helpful with return to work while lack of support has been a barrier to return to work.8, 9 ● Some cancer survivors may be reluctant to state their rights according to the law for fears that this may negatively impact their employer-employee relationship.

Clinical Tip

Supervisors may need to be guided by those who are knowledgeable about the employer's duty to accommodate and relevant legislation, such as human resources professionals, disability managers, return to work coordinators, and union representatives. In some cases, supervisors and employers of small businesses may not be aware of their obligation in regards to human rights and work accommodations.10 For those who do not have access to guidance from such experts, legal resources available can be found on Cancer and Work: Legal Resources

To identify and foster workplace supports, primary care providers can:
  • Provide a letter, fill out forms, or directly communicate with the workplace regarding the individual’s fitness and readiness for return to work (RTW)
  • Encourage cancer survivors to discuss and determine how best to address RTW with their employer in a timely manner and with the cancer survivor's consent
  • Inquire about the level of support an employer is able and ready to provide, and tailor RTW plan accordingly

    • Examples of questions you can ask ▼

      • What supports and accommodations An employer has a duty to reasonably accommodate on an ongoing basis those with a disability unless the employer can prove undue hardship. The duty to accommodate means that employers must implement the necessary measures that will allow employees with limitations due to illness or disability to work to the best of their ability. The principle of accommodations to the needs of people with an illness or disability includes cancer survivors.

        For more information see Cancer and Work: Reasonable Accommodation         are routinely offered? What have others received post-illness and/or injury?
      • What accommodation is the employer willing to provide? (i.e. graduated return to work, flexible hours, working from home)
      • What timeline is the employer willing to accept for a graduate RTW?
  • Refer to counselling or social work services to address the cancer survivor’s challenges with setting boundaries and assertiveness
  • Refer to vocational rehabilitation, social work, or counselling services if the cancer survivor is reluctant to speak to the employer
  • Share resources to support survivors' understanding of how to exercise their power of disclosure
  • If the employer is reluctant to provide accommodations, encourage the cancer survivor to review legal answers or consult their local human rights organization on employers' rights to medical information

pages.title: iCanWork Step 9: Manage Work Expectations
pages.content:
For some cancer survivors, recovery may take time, while for others, there may be permanent changes in their physical, psychological, cognitive and functional abilities. Some cancer survivors may experience invisible barriers to work such as fatigue, psychological challenges, pain, or cognitive problems. These symptoms represent unseen considerations that may be harder for people in the workplace to understand or accept.

Role of Primary Care

Primary care providers can help cancer survivors manage work-related expectations by:

  • Discussing what recovery over time may look like
  • Provide clear guidelines for restrictions and limitations in their return to work (RTW) plan
  • Encouraging survivors to refer back to the RTW plan and medical guidance if challenged by their employer/manager about work ability or if asked to work longer hours than outlined
  • Referring to counselling services to address fears, set boundaries, and develop assertiveness if survivors are feeling vulnerable

Clinical Tip

Returning to work may also require readjusting other roles and routines, such as managing tasks at home and adjusting social activities to reduce contributors to fatigue. As no two people are the same, it is important to consider each individual in context, in order to best understand and facilitate their unique RTW needs.

Despite laws obliging employers to accommodate those with disabilities, some employers can be quite rigid about time limits for a graduated return to work plan and this needs to be determined as part of creating a RTW plan.

Return to work (RTW) plans are co-developed by an employer and cancer survivor with input from other parties involved in the RTW process (i.e. healthcare providers). Plans should be individualized and flexible to meet each survivor’s unique needs and the employer’s ability to provide accommodations.1, 2

Ideally, RTW plans are given to the cancer survivor in writing so that they can give the document to their insurance provider, supervisor, and any other staff member who can help them with their RTW.

Workplace Accommodations

Recommendations can include exploring with cancer survivors job accommodation ideas that they think can help improve their transition to work and optimize their productivity. The most helpful accommodations described by survivors, employers and health care providers are: graduated return to work, flexible scheduling, modification of physical work environment and provision of adaptive aids, modification of workplace duties and performance expectations and retraining and supports at the workplace3.

courseSummary: Assessment of cancer survivors' abilities in relation to their work demands is needed to determine potential challenges with return to work and the need for referral to specialists.
Referrals or recommendations for funding may be required to access medical and allied health specialists to address challenges related to return to work.

Regular encouragement of cancer survivors to play an active role in their return to work process is recommended to assist in empowering them to develop resiliency skills and optimize their health and well-being.
The transition to returning to work is aided when cancer survivors maintain positive communication and ongoing dialogue with their employer regarding their return to work plans.
Workplace expectations can be managed by medical and allied health specialists by providing medical opinions on work restrictions and limitations and the return to work plan.

A return to work plan should be individualized to fit the cancer survivors’ unique needs, flexible to respond to ongoing and new challenges, and include feedback from all parties involved (primary care providers, referred specialists, cancer survivor, and employer).
